title: Hanna-Barbera
description: American animation studio and production company
wiki_lead:
Hanna-Barbera Cartoons, Inc. ( bar-BAIR-ə; also known simply as Hanna Barbera, and formerly known as H-B Enterprises, Hanna-Barbera Productions, Inc. and H-B Production Co.) was an American animation studio and production company that operated from 1957 until its absorption into Warner Bros. Animation in 2001. The studio was founded on July 7, 1957, by William Hanna and Joseph Barbera, the creators of Tom and Jerry and former MGM Cartoons employees, along with film producer George Sidney. Initially headquartered at Kling Studios in Los Angeles from 1957 to 1960, the company later moved to Cahuenga Boulevard until 1998, and finally to the Sherman Oaks Galleria in Sherman Oaks from 1998 to 2001.
Hanna-Barbera was known for producing a vast array of animated series, including Huckleberry Hound, all iterations of The Flintstones, Yogi Bear, Jonny Quest, Scooby-Doo, Super Friends, and The Smurfs. However, by the 1980s, the studio's dominance declined as the market for Saturday-morning cartoons weakened, and weekday syndication grew in importance. Hanna-Barbera was acquired by Taft Broadcasting in 1966 and remained under its ownership until 1991, when Turner Broadcasting System purchased the company. Turner used Hanna-Barbera's extensive back catalog to help launch Cartoon Network in 1992, giving a new platform for the studio's classic animated properties.
After William Hanna died in 2001, Hanna-Barbera ceased to exist as an independent studio and was fully integrated into Warner Bros. Animation. Hanna-Barbera continues to exist as an in-name-only unit of Skydance managing copyright, marketing, and branding purposes of properties created during Hanna-Barbera's existence.

History


Tom and Jerry and birth of a studio (1938–1957)
William Denby "Bill" Hanna and Joseph Roland "Joe" Barbera met at the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (MGM) studio in 1938, while working at its animation unit. Having worked at other studios since the early 1930s, they solidified a six-decade working partnership. Tom and Jerry, their very first collaborative success, came about in 1940, centering on the madcap comical adventures of a cat and a mouse. Hanna supervised the animation, while Barbera did the stories and pre-production for all 114 cartoons. Seven of the films won seven Oscars for "Best Short Subject (Cartoons)" between 1943 and 1953, and five additional shorts were nominated for twelve awards during this period. However, they were awarded to producer Fred Quimby, who was not directly involved in the development of the shorts. With Quimby's retirement in May 1955, Hanna and Barbera became the producers in charge of the MGM animation studio's output.
In addition to continuing to write and direct new Tom & Jerry shorts, now in CinemaScope, Hanna and Barbera produced the last seven shorts of Tex Avery's Droopy series, directed by Michael Lah, and produced and directed the short-lived Spike and Tyke, which ran for two entries. grok_lead: Hanna-Barbera Productions was an American animation studio founded on July 7, 1957, by animators William Hanna and Joseph Barbera in Los Angeles, California, following the closure of MGM's animation department in 1957 where the duo had created the acclaimed Tom and Jerry series. The studio pioneered cost-effective limited animation techniques for television, producing over 100 series and more than 3,000 half-hours of programming that dominated Saturday morning cartoons and introduced prime-time animated sitcoms. Under Hanna and Barbera's leadership, the studio debuted with The Ruff and Reddy Show in 1957, followed by breakthroughs like The Huckleberry Hound Show in 1958, which introduced characters such as Yogi Bear and earned the first Emmy Award for an animated television series in 1960. The Flintstones, launched in 1960 as the first animated series in prime-time network television, satirized suburban life with Stone Age settings and ran for six seasons, spawning merchandise and cultural impact. Other iconic productions included The Jetsons (1962â1963), a futuristic family comedy; Jonny Quest (1964); Scooby-Doo, Where Are You! (1969), which became a long-running mystery franchise; and The Smurfs (1981â1989), based on the Belgian comics and one of the most-watched children's shows of the 1980s. The company's ownership evolved through several acquisitions: Taft Broadcasting purchased it in 1967 for $12 million, expanding its scope into live-action and theme parks; Great American Broadcasting acquired it in 1987 amid financial restructuring; Turner Broadcasting System bought it in 1991 for $320 million, integrating its library into the newly launched Cartoon Network in 1992; and following the 1996 Time Warner merger, it was absorbed into Warner Bros. Animation in 2001, effectively ending the original studio while preserving the brand for licensing and new content. In 2021, WarnerMedia (now Warner Bros. Discovery) revived the Hanna-Barbera name as Hanna-Barbera Studios Europe in London. As of 2025, it focuses on regional animation projects like The Amazing World of Gumball spin-offs and DC-inspired shorts, including new developments such as the adult animated series Hit Squad, continuing the legacy of innovative storytelling for global audiences.
